questions.question: How many aircraft and live write-ups should the app be designed for?

options.label: Small fleet (Recommended)
options.description: Roughly 10–30 aircraft and tens of open write-ups. Render full lists with no pagination, in a local database. Tradeoff: at real airline scale (hundreds of aircraft, thousands of items) you'd need pagination, filtering and indexes.

options.label: Airline scale
options.description: Build pagination, search and indexes from the start. Spends time on problems the demo data won't have.

questions.question: What exactly decides whether an aircraft is 'cleared to fly'?

options.label: Any unresolved High (Recommended)
options.description: Grounded the moment a High write-up is filed, with no triage delay, and stays grounded until every High on that aircraft is resolved. Medium and Low never ground, even when overdue. This is the literal reading of the brief and errs on the side of safety. Cleared status is computed from open write-ups, never stored separately, so it can't drift.

options.label: Also ground on overdue Medium
options.description: Stricter, but it invents a rule the brief doesn't state.

options.label: Ground only once High is confirmed
options.description: A mechanic triages before the aircraft is grounded. Less conservative: an aircraft with an unconfirmed High could fly. Also adds a state.

questions.question: Can a write-up's severity be changed after it's filed, for example a mechanic downgrading a High to Medium after inspection, which would clear the aircraft?

options.label: Yes, with a required reason (Recommended)
options.description: First reports are often over- or under-graded. A downgrade from High is the safety-critical moment because it clears an aircraft, so require a name and reason, which goes into the audit log you chose. Grounding is recalculated immediately. Costs one small form and a validation.

options.label: Yes, freely editable
options.description: Simpler, but an aircraft can be silently cleared by an unexplained edit (the audit log would still show who did it).

options.label: No, fixed at filing
options.description: Simplest. A wrongly graded write-up has to be resolved and filed again, which is clunky and misrepresents what happened.

questions.question: The brief says the app 'shows at any moment which aircraft are cleared to fly.' Does that mean live push updates, or always-correct status whenever you look?

options.label: Correct on every load (Recommended)
options.description: Status is computed from current data on every request and after every action. No websockets or polling. Tradeoff: two people looking at once see each other's changes only after a refresh.

options.label: Periodic polling
options.description: The page re-fetches every few seconds. Cheap-ish and feels live, but adds client code and wastes requests.

options.label: Live push
options.description: Websockets or server-sent events. Most real-time, and the most infrastructure and moving parts in a two-hour build.

**Decision:** No. Status is correct whenever a page loads or an action is taken. Other users' changes appear on refresh.
**Why:** Start simple. If there's time at the end, add live push then.

questions.question: How does a write-up close when the mechanic finds nothing wrong (can't reproduce the fault) or it duplicates another write-up?

options.label: Resolve with a note (Recommended)
options.description: Uses the same Resolved state, with the required note saying 'could not duplicate' or 'duplicate of #12'. No extra state. Tradeoff: reports can't tell real fixes apart from no-fault closures without reading the notes.

options.label: Separate 'Closed, no fault' outcome
options.description: Resolved carries an outcome (Fixed or No fault found). Cleaner data, but one more field and branch to handle and test.

options.label: Allow deleting write-ups
options.description: Simplest for duplicates, but deleting maintenance records undermines the audit log you chose. Not recommended.

questions.question: What happens when a write-up's scheduled repair date passes and it still isn't resolved?

options.label: Flag as overdue (Recommended)
options.description: Show a computed 'Overdue' badge so maintenance control can see slipped work. Doesn't affect whether the aircraft can fly, consistent with the grounding rule. Small cost: one date comparison plus a test.

options.label: No overdue concept
options.description: Simplest, but a slipped date just sits quietly as 'Scheduled', which undermines 'every issue needs to be scheduled'.

questions.question: Does the app need screens to add, edit or remove aircraft, or is the fleet fixed seed data?

options.label: Seeded fleet only (Recommended)
options.description: The brief says to make up the data. CRUD screens for aircraft are plumbing that doesn't show product judgment. Tradeoff: adding an aircraft means editing the seed.

options.label: Add aircraft in the UI
options.description: A small form to add tail numbers. Realistic, but time spent off the core flow.

questions.question: Real airlines can defer some non-critical defects under a Minimum Equipment List (MEL) and fly with them for a limited time. Should the app model deferrals?

options.label: Out of scope (Recommended)
options.description: The brief's rule is simple, and Medium and Low already don't ground. Document it as a known simplification and next step. Modeling deferral categories and time limits is a domain rabbit hole.

options.label: Model deferral limits
options.description: More realistic airworthiness, but it means designing rules the brief doesn't give, at real risk to the time budget.

[DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md) now records all 16 questions, nine of yours and seven of mine, and it's committed locally but not pushed. Where you went against my recommendation it's noted: the In progress stage, the full audit log, designing for a fleet 10x to 50x bigger, and the Canceled state. Some things to push back on before we build:

- **Scope is growing.** Each of those four calls is small, but together they add a state, an event table written on every change, and an extra closed state. The audit log costs the most. It stays manageable if every change goes through one function that both updates the write-up and appends the event. If changes are written from several places, it will eat the time budget.
- **Canceling a High clears the aircraft.** That's the same risky moment as downgrading a High's severity, which we decided needs a name and a reason. The required note covers part of it. I'd also require a name, for consistency, but that's your call and it isn't recorded yet.

- **Allowed transitions are still undecided.** For example, can Unscheduled go straight to In progress? Can Scheduled go back to Unscheduled? Is rescheduling allowed? Which states can be Canceled from? These are your core correctness tests, so I'd settle them before writing code.

questions.question: Can an Unscheduled write-up go straight to In progress (a mechanic fixes it on the spot), or must it be Scheduled first?

options.label: Must be Scheduled first (Recommended)
options.description: Strictly linear flow: every write-up gets a date, which literally satisfies 'every issue needs to be scheduled', and there are fewer transitions to test. Tradeoff: a quick ramp fix means picking today's date first, one extra step.

options.label: Allow skipping to In progress
options.description: Faster for quick fixes, but then some write-ups never get a scheduled date, so Overdue and 'needs scheduling' have more cases to handle.

questions.question: Once a write-up is Scheduled, can its date be changed, and can it go back to Unscheduled?

options.label: Reschedule only (Recommended)
options.description: The date can move (logged in the audit log), but it can't go back to Unscheduled. Plans slip all the time; dropping the date entirely just hides the work again. Tradeoff: an item really bumped indefinitely needs a placeholder date.

options.label: Reschedule and unschedule
options.description: Most flexible. Adds a backwards transition, and the 'needs scheduling' queue can fill back up.

options.label: Date is fixed once set
options.description: Simplest, but unrealistic. A slipped date would mean canceling and filing again.

questions.question: Can an In progress write-up go back to Scheduled, for example when work stops while waiting on parts?

options.label: Yes, with a new date (Recommended)
options.description: Waiting on parts is the most common reason maintenance stalls. Going back to Scheduled with a new date keeps the Overdue flag meaningful. Costs one backwards transition and a test.

options.label: No, stays In progress
options.description: Simpler. A stalled item sits In progress with a past date and shows as Overdue, which is arguably accurate but hides the reason.

questions.question: Can a write-up be Resolved directly from Scheduled, or only from In progress?

options.label: Only from In progress (Recommended)
options.description: Keeps the flow strictly linear and gives the In progress state you chose a real job. Tradeoff: two clicks to finish a quick fix (Start, then Resolve).

options.label: From Scheduled or In progress
options.description: Saves a click, but In progress becomes optional, so it's less reliable as a signal of work that's actually underway.

# Decisions

## Questions for the product manager

### 1. Can a write-up be filed without a repair date?
**Decision:** Yes. A write-up can be filed without a date and starts as Unscheduled.

### 2. What stages does a write-up move through?
**Decision:** Unscheduled → Scheduled → In progress → Resolved.
**Note:** Went against the AI recommendation, which was to leave out In progress.

### 3. Does a fix need a separate inspection or certification sign-off?
**Decision:** No separate stage. Resolving a write-up records who fixed it and what was done.

### 4. Can a resolved write-up be reopened?
**Decision:** No. A recurring defect is filed as a new write-up.

### 5. Who are the users, and do views differ by role?
**Decision:** One shared view for pilots, mechanics and maintenance control, with no roles and no login. People type their names where it matters (reporter, fixer).

### 6. Who is a write-up assigned to?
**Decision:** Nobody. A scheduled date is enough, and the fixer's name is recorded when the write-up is resolved.

### 7. Do we store and display a history of who changed what and when?
**Decision:** Yes, a full audit log of every change to each write-up.
**Note:** Went against the AI recommendation, which was to store only key timestamps on the write-up itself.

### 8. Any categorization besides severity and status?
**Decision:** No. The defect is a free-text description.

### 9. How many aircraft and live write-ups should the app handle?
**Decision:** Designed for a fleet of about 30 aircraft, but it shouldn't fall over if the fleet grew 10x to 50x (roughly 300 to 1,500 aircraft).
**Note:** Went further than the AI recommendation, which was to design only for a small fleet and accept that scaling later would need rework.

### 10. What decides whether an aircraft is cleared to fly?
**Decision:** Any unresolved High write-up grounds the aircraft, from the moment it's filed until every High on that aircraft is resolved. Medium and Low never ground, even when overdue. Cleared status is computed from open write-ups, never stored.

### 11. Can severity be changed after filing?
**Decision:** Yes, but changing it requires a name and a reason, which are recorded in the audit log. Grounding is recalculated immediately.

### 12. Does "at any moment" mean live push updates?
**Decision:** No. Status is correct whenever a page loads or an action is taken. Other users' changes appear on refresh.
**Why:** Start simple. If there's time at the end, add live push then.

### 13. How does a write-up close when there's no fault to fix, or it's a duplicate?
**Decision:** A separate Canceled state, with a required note. This adds to the stages in question 2.
**Note:** Went against the AI recommendation, which was to reuse Resolved with a note.

### 14. What happens when a scheduled repair date passes?
**Decision:** The write-up is flagged Overdue. That flag is computed and doesn't affect whether the aircraft can fly.

### 15. Can aircraft be added or edited in the app?
**Decision:** Not for now; the fleet is seed data. Managing aircraft in the UI is a candidate to pick up at the end if there's time.

### 16. Should the app model MEL deferrals?
**Decision:** No, that's out of scope.

**Decision:** Any unresolved High write-up grounds the aircraft, from the moment it's filed until every High on that aircraft is resolved. Medium and Low never ground, even when overdue. Cleared status is computed from open write-ups, never stored.

### 11. Can severity be changed after filing?
**Decision:** Yes, but changing it requires a name and a reason, which are recorded in the audit log. Grounding is recalculated immediately.

### 12. Does "at any moment" mean live push updates?
**Decision:** No. Status is correct whenever a page loads or an action is taken. Other users' changes appear on refresh.
**Why:** Start simple. If there's time at the end, add live push then.

### 13. How does a write-up close when there's no fault to fix, or it's a duplicate?
**Decision:** A separate Canceled state, with a required note. This adds to the stages in question 2.
**Note:** Went against the AI recommendation, which was to reuse Resolved with a note.

### 14. What happens when a scheduled repair date passes?
**Decision:** The write-up is flagged Overdue. That flag is computed and doesn't affect whether the aircraft can fly.

### 15. Can aircraft be added or edited in the app?
**Decision:** Not for now; the fleet is seed data. Managing aircraft in the UI is a candidate to pick up at the end if there's time.

### 16. Should the app model MEL deferrals?
**Decision:** No, that's out of scope.

### 17. Can an Unscheduled write-up go straight to In progress?
**Decision:** No. It must be Scheduled first.

### 18. Once Scheduled, can the date change or the write-up go back to Unscheduled?
**Decision:** Both. The date can be changed, and a Scheduled write-up can go back to Unscheduled.
**Note:** Went against the AI recommendation, which was to allow rescheduling only.

### 19. Can an In progress write-up go back to Scheduled (e.g. waiting on parts)?
**Decision:** No. It stays In progress, but its scheduled date can still be changed. The scheduled date is the date the repair should be *finished by*, not the day work starts. A multi-day repair might go In progress on Monday with a scheduled date of Friday.
**Note:** Went against the AI recommendation, which was to allow going back to Scheduled with a new date.

### 20. Can a write-up be Resolved directly from Scheduled?
**Decision:** No. Only an In progress write-up can be Resolved.

content.text:
Decisions 17–23 are in [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md) and committed locally (not pushed). Here is the full state model they add up to, which will drive the core tests:

| From | Allowed transitions |
|---|---|
| Unscheduled | → Scheduled (needs a date, today or later) · → Canceled |
| Scheduled | → In progress · → Unscheduled (clears the date) · reschedule · → Canceled |
| In progress | → Resolved (needs a name and a note on the work) · reschedule · → Canceled |
| Resolved / Canceled | final |

Three things apply in any open state:
- Severity can change, with a name and a reason.
- The description can be edited.
- Every change goes in the audit log.

**Two things to flag:**

- **"Scheduled date" is the wrong name now.** You've defined it as the date the repair should be *finished by*, so I'd call it `due_date` in the code and the UI. That also makes Overdue read naturally: due date passed and not resolved or canceled. I'll make that rename when we write the model unless you say otherwise.
- **"Unscheduled" sits oddly next to the date rules.** Scheduled can go back to Unscheduled, but In progress can't go back to anything, and both can have their date changed. That's consistent with what you chose, just worth knowing: an In progress item always has a due date, but a Scheduled one can lose its date.
